newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: British foreign minister cuts short HK visit.
newsitem.headline: British foreign minister cuts short HK visit.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Saturday he would cut short a visit to Hong Kong to get back to London in time for a key parliamentary vote.
Rifkind, in Singapore for a meeting of Asian and European foreign ministers, was originally scheduled to fly to Hong Kong on Saturday evening and return home on Tuesday.
"I am leaving this conference earlier in order to be able to fly home on Monday morning," he told reporters.

Rifkind said he had moved his trip forward slightly and shortened it to enable him to return for the parliamentary vote, called by the opposition Labour Party over Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's handling of the "mad cow" crisis.
Prime Minister John Major's beleaguered Conservative administration needs all available hands present for the vote, which is likely to be close.
"I'm bringing the visit forward slightly because of the need to be also in the House of Commons early next week," he told reporters.
"So we are rearranging the programme. But I've got a very full programme (in Hong Kong) both this evening and tomorrow and I am looking forward to that," he added.
He was scheduled to meet Governor Chris Patten and Tung Chee-hwa, the man selected by a pro-Beijing commitee to run Hong Kong after Britain hands the colony back to China at midnight on June 30.
The meeting with Tung had been planned for Monday.
Asked if he would still meet Tung, Rifkind said:

"Yes, certainly. That has been part of the programme and I am looking forward to seeing him again. I have met him on previous occasions. We have corresponded and I am looking forward to a full discussion with him tomorrow."
A senior British official told Reuters that Rifkind had brought forward all his meetings in Hong Kong.
"His meetings with the Governor and the chief executive-designate and others will take place on Saturday evening and Sunday," he said.
Rifkind was due to arrive in Hong Kong at 6.00 pm (1000 GMT) on Saturday, British officials said.
One said it was "extremely inconvenient" for Rifkind to cut short his trip to Hong Kong, his last official visit before the handover ceremony on June 30.
Rifkind had expected to be able to ignore the vote in London because the Labour Party's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, had also been due to visit Singapore on Monday, the officials said.
But political party managers in London summoned all their members of parliament to attend Monday night's vote and Cook cancelled the visit.
The Conservatives have the same number of parliamentary seats as all opposition parties combined, although they have 51 seats more than second-place Labour.

If Labour were to win the vote, generally considered unlikely, Hogg would be forced to resign and a vote of no-confidence in Major's government could be triggered. Major's position would then be precarious.
Labour is around 20 points ahead in opinion polls and Major must hold a general election by May 22. He is believed to favour May 1 but might be forced to hold an earlier poll.
